editor.title: The editor
editor.summary: The notation canvas, the caret, and how notes get written.

canvas.heading: The canvas
canvas.p1: The score is drawn onto a single canvas, and only the systems you can see are drawn on any frame. That is what lets a long score stay responsive — the cost of drawing does not grow with the number of bars.
canvas.p2: Down the left of every system is the track gutter: each track's name, its instrument, and its mute and solo controls. It is painted into the same canvas as the staves, so it can never drift out of alignment with the music it labels.
canvas.p3: A track that is not the one you are editing dims — notes, beams, ties and stave lines together — so which part you are working on reads at a glance. A selected note keeps its colour on every track, because selecting across tracks is something you did on purpose.

caret.heading: The caret and selection
caret.p1: The red caret is where the next note goes and where playback starts. Clicking empty staff moves it, makes that track active and clears the selection; clicking a note also selects that note.
caret.p2: Shift-click adds or removes a note from the selection. Cmd-click selects everything from the caret to where you clicked on the active track, and Cmd-Shift-click does the same across every track.
caret.p3: The bar numbers above each system are a gutter of their own: click one to select that bar, shift-click to extend the selection to a span of bars. Replace and regeneration both work on spans, so this is how you aim them.

noteInput.heading: Writing notes
noteInput.p1: There are four ways to write a note: type its letter, click the staff with note input on, play the on-screen piano, or play a connected MIDI keyboard.
noteInput.p2: Typing is usually quickest. A to G writes that note at the caret in the octave nearest the note before it, so a melody does not have to be transposed after the fact. Digits 1 to 6 choose the note value, a full stop dots it, R writes a rest and T ties.
noteInput.p3: Note input is a mode, toggled with N, because a click has to be able to mean two things: with it off a click aims the caret, with it on a click writes a note at the pitch you clicked.

editModes.heading: Insert, replace and stack
editModes.p1: Insert pushes the track's later notes out of the way to make room. Replace overwrites whatever was already there. Stack adds the note to what is already at that position, building a chord.
editModes.p2: Stack is unavailable on an instrument that can only sound one note at a time — a flute cannot play a chord, and the toolbar says so rather than letting you write one.

voices.heading: Voices
voices.p1: A stave can carry two independent voices. They are told apart by their stems: the upper voice points up and the lower points down, which is what an engraver would do.
voices.p2: A single voice keeps the renderer's own stem choice, because forcing a direction there would point half the notes the wrong way.

layout.heading: Layout and zoom
layout.p1: Page layout wraps the music into systems that fit the width, the way printed music does. Continuous layout lays the whole score out as one long system and scrolls sideways.
layout.p2: Zoom scales the engraving. It changes how much fits on screen, never what is in the score.

formats.title: Import and export
formats.summary: What the app reads, what it writes, and what survives the trip.

importing.heading: Importing
importing.p1: Every import makes a new project, which is why they all live on the Projects page rather than inside the editor — an import from an open score could only throw you out of it.
importing.p2: The one exception is audio brought in as a track rather than a project. That writes a transcription onto the score you already have, so it sits under Add Track in the editor instead.
importing.p3: A tracker module is chosen by its contents rather than its file name, so a mis-named module still imports and an unrecognised file fails by saying what it actually found.

exporting.heading: Exporting
exporting.p1: The Export menu writes MIDI, MusicXML, an XM tracker module, audio as WAV or MP3, and the project as a project file. Print is separate, and offers Letter or Legal in portrait or landscape.
exporting.p2: Audio is rendered through the same soundfont that plays it, so the file is a recording of what you heard rather than a second interpretation.
exporting.p3: If the score has hidden tracks, exporting asks whether to include them rather than quietly deciding for you.

fidelity.heading: What survives
fidelity.p1: MIDI carries what the transport played, not what is stored — dynamics, hairpins, articulation and grace notes all reach the file. MusicXML carries the engraving: beams, slurs, ornaments, lyrics, repeats and navigation marks.
fidelity.p2: A tracker module is the lossiest of the three, and says so before writing: it has a row grid, a channel limit and a note range, and the export shows you what would be lost before it writes anything.

in.midi: Notes, tempo and time signatures. You choose how it is split into tracks and how tightly it is quantized.
in.musicxml: The engraving as well as the notes: beams, slurs, ornaments, lyrics, repeats and clef changes.
in.tracker: Notes grouped by instrument rather than by channel, so a part played across channels lands on one track.
in.audio: One line at a time. Monophonic only — chords and mixes are not attempted, and the dialog says so.
in.project: A whole project exactly as it was exported, including every track and its mix.

out.midi: What the transport played, including dynamics, hairpins, articulation and grace notes.
out.musicxml: The full engraving, for opening in other notation software.
out.tracker: Notes only. Instrument slots are named but empty, so the file is silent until a tracker user fills them.
out.wav: Uncompressed audio, rendered through the same soundfont that plays it.
out.mp3: Compressed audio, from the same render.
out.project: Everything, for backup or for moving between accounts.
out.print: A print view with paper size and orientation, for printing or saving as PDF.

generation.title: Music generation
generation.summary: Generating a score, a track, or a replacement — and what it costs.

whole.heading: Generating a score
whole.p1: From the Projects page, describe what you want and choose the instruments, the length, the tempo, the key and the meter. Anything you leave blank the generator decides for itself.
whole.p2: Generation runs on the server, not in your browser. You can close the page and come back — the project shows its progress and the result is applied when it lands.
whole.p3: The first instrument you list is the one that carries the melody, which is why the order of the list matters.

track.heading: Generating a track
track.p1: Inside the editor you can add one track to a score you already have. It is given the score's key, tempo and length, and the other parts to fit around.
track.p2: That last part matters: the generator is shown what the existing tracks are playing over the same bars, so a bass line is written under your melody rather than beside it.

replace.heading: Replacing music
replace.p1: Replace rewrites part of a score you already have. Select some bars and replace those; select a track and replace all of it; or select individual notes and replace just them.
replace.p2: You can hold parts of it steady while the rest changes — keep the harmony, keep the rhythm, keep the melody and vary the accompaniment, or keep the notes at the edges so the new music joins on cleanly.
replace.p3: Replacing notes is the one case that is not rounded out to whole bars. The selection is replaced as the span it covers, and the dialog says how many notes inside that span were not selected.

credits.heading: What it costs
credits.p1: One credit writes one bar for one instrument. Eight bars for four instruments is 32 credits. The dialog shows an estimate before you commit.
credits.p2: The estimate says about, because you are charged for what was actually produced. That matches the estimate when generation returns the length you asked for, and is smaller otherwise.

quality.heading: How the result is checked
quality.p1: Every generated part is checked before you see it: notes outside the instrument's range, notes that would be silent, duplicate notes at the same moment, chords the instrument cannot play, and parts with no rhythmic or dynamic variety at all.
quality.p2: If something is wrong the generator is asked again, and told exactly what to fix rather than simply asked to try once more. It is bounded, so a stubborn request does not run away.
quality.p3: A remaining problem never throws the result away. The best attempt is kept and the problem is reported, because a part that needs a small edit is worth more than nothing at all.

getting-started.title: Getting started
getting-started.summary: What this app is, and how to get a score in front of you.

what.heading: What it is
what.p1: Moosiac is a notation editor with AI generation attached. You describe the music you want and it writes a score; from there every note is yours to edit, play back, print and export.
what.p2: Nothing is generated that you cannot then change by hand. The generator writes into the same score model the editor uses, so a generated bar and a bar you typed are the same kind of thing.

firstProject.heading: Making your first project
firstProject.p1: Everything starts on the Projects page. There are four ways to begin: start from a template, generate a whole score with AI, import a file, or duplicate a project you already have.
firstProject.p2: Templates are empty scores with the staves already set up — a lead sheet, a piano grand staff, a string quartet, a jazz combo. They are the fastest way to a blank page that is the right shape.
firstProject.p3: Importing makes a project too. A MIDI file, a MusicXML file, a tracker module, an audio recording or a project file all land as a new project rather than merging into an open one.

dashboard.heading: The Projects page
dashboard.p1: Projects are listed newest first and can be sorted by name or searched. Each row opens the editor, and the menu on it duplicates or deletes.
dashboard.p2: A project being generated shows its progress in place and can be cancelled there. You can leave the page — generation runs on the server, not in your browser.

inspector.title: The inspector
inspector.summary: The property panel: track, note, bar and score.

tabs.heading: The four tabs
tabs.p1: Track is first because it always has something to show — there is always an active track. It holds the name, the instrument or drum kit, the clef, volume, pan, mute and solo, and deleting the track.
tabs.p2: Note shows what is selected: pitch, accidental, octave, duration, velocity, voice, articulation, ornament, dynamic, chord symbol, fingering, and the spans — slur, glissando, octave bracket.
tabs.p3: Bar covers the one you selected: its number, time and key signature, a tempo change starting here, barline style, repeats and endings, a clef change, the navigation marks and whether it is a pickup.
tabs.p4: Score is the piece itself — its title, composer and description. The title names every exported file, and it is not the same thing as the project name that labels the row on the Projects page.

editing.heading: Reading it
editing.p1: The panel says note values, bar numbers and key names rather than ticks and fifths. A quarter note reads as a quarter note, not as 480.
editing.p2: Where several selected notes disagree about a value, the field shows that they are mixed rather than picking one of them to display.

instruments.title: Instruments
instruments.summary: The 128 General MIDI programs, their compasses, and how far to trust them.

catalogue.heading: The catalogue
catalogue.p1: A track's sound is one of the 128 General MIDI programs, grouped into sixteen families of eight. Each program carries its own compass, how many notes it can sound at once, and how far its written pitch sits from its sounding pitch.
catalogue.p2: The table below is generated from that data rather than written out, so it cannot fall out of step with what the app actually uses.
catalogue.p3: Transposition is shown in semitones from sounding to written. A B-flat trumpet reads +2: a sounding C is written as a D. An empty cell means the instrument is written where it sounds, which is most of them.

compass.heading: How far to trust a compass
compass.p1: The last column is the one worth reading. Measured means somebody checked that instrument against a source. Tunable means the instrument has no fixed absolute pitch at all — a shamisen is tuned to the singer, a koto to the piece — so the range shown is a typical span rather than a limit.
compass.p2: Synthetic means an electronic patch, which has no acoustic compass to respect, so it gets the whole keyboard rather than an invented limit. Unpitched means a sound effect or an untuned percussion sound: there is no pitch to be outside of.
compass.p3: Only a measured compass is ever used to refuse a note. Refusing against a range nobody verified would reject music that was perfectly fine, so the app does not do it.

percussion.heading: Drums
percussion.p1: A percussion track works differently: the pitch names a drum rather than a note. Middle C is a kick drum, the D above it a snare. The map covers MIDI 35 to 81 and anything outside it makes no sound.
percussion.p2: On a drum track the instrument field selects a kit rather than an instrument. General MIDI defines eight — Standard, Room, Power, Electronic, TR-808, Jazz, Brush and Orchestra — and the same number means a kit here and an instrument everywhere else.
percussion.p3: The on-screen keyboard labels every drum key so you do not have to learn the map.

instruments.search: Search by name, family or program number

limits.title: Limits and known gaps
limits.summary: What the app deliberately does not do, and what it does not do yet.

byDesign.heading: By design
byDesign.p1: Audio import is monophonic. One line at a time — chords and mixes are not attempted, and the dialog says so rather than producing a confident wrong answer.
byDesign.p2: Generation returns one result and applies it. There is no candidate list to choose between, because generation runs as a background job and nobody is looking when it lands.
byDesign.p3: Snapshots cannot be edited or deleted. Immutability is enforced by there being no operation to do it, rather than by a rule that has to be remembered.

known.heading: Known gaps
known.p1: Beaming cannot be joined across a beat, only broken or removed. A file that beams across a beat imports with our grouping rather than its own.
known.p2: Ornaments are drawn and exported but not played. The sign is primarily notational, and realising it would make the ornament impossible to re-read afterwards.
known.p3: A tracker module is written with notes only. Its instrument slots are named but empty, so the file is silent until a tracker user fills them in — the export says so before it writes.

midi-input.title: MIDI keyboards
midi-input.summary: Playing notes in from a connected instrument.

connecting.heading: Connecting
connecting.p1: A MIDI keyboard connected to your computer can play notes straight into the score. Access is requested the first time devices are listed, not when the page loads, so you are never prompted for a permission you may not need.
connecting.p2: It works wherever the browser supports Web MIDI. Where it does not, the feature is simply not offered rather than failing when you try it.
connecting.p3: No sysex access is requested — only the note messages the editor actually uses.

playing.heading: Playing in
playing.p1: Notes from a MIDI keyboard go through exactly the same path as the on-screen keys: the note sounds while held, a chord struck together is grouped, how long you held it becomes the duration, and the caret advances past what was written.
playing.p2: Many keyboards send a note-on at zero velocity instead of a note-off. That is read as a release, because taking it literally would leave the note sounding forever.

navigation.title: Getting around
navigation.summary: The pages, what each is for, and which need an account.

routes.heading: The pages
routes.p1: The top bar carries Projects, Community, Docs, Resources and Settings. The logo returns to the home page. Everything sits under a language prefix, so the English site is /en and the Chinese one is /zh.
routes.p2: Projects is your own work. Community is what other people have shared. Resources points at free archives worth importing from. Settings holds theme, text size, how pitch is displayed, and the developer options.
routes.p3: Opening a project takes you to the editor at /project/its-id. Print is a separate view at /project/its-id/print, and a shared snapshot reads at /p/its-public-id.

account.heading: What needs an account
account.p1: Projects, credits and purchases need you to be signed in. Home, Community, Docs, Resources, Settings and any shared snapshot do not.
account.p2: That last one is deliberate: a link you share has to open for someone who has never signed in, so the published reader is outside the sign-in gate entirely.

notation.title: Marks and notation
notation.summary: Everything you can write on a note beyond its pitch and length.

ties.heading: Ties and rests
ties.p1: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one sounding note. Select a note and press T, or use the toolbar. A tie is not a slur — it joins, where a slur only phrases.
ties.p2: You never write a rest to make silence. Silence is simply the space you leave between notes, and rests appear where the gaps are. R writes one explicitly when you want to occupy a beat deliberately.

dynamics.heading: Dynamics and hairpins
dynamics.p1: A dynamic marks the level a passage begins at, from ppp to fff, and stays in force until the next one. Marking one note f makes the whole passage loud — there is nothing to apply to the notes between.
dynamics.p2: The note's own velocity survives as a deviation on top of that level, so an accent inside a quiet passage stays an accent rather than being flattened.
dynamics.p3: A hairpin is the change between two levels, written over two or more notes with Shift+< or Shift+>. It sounds as a ramp, moving to whatever marking follows it, or by one step where nothing follows.

articulation.heading: Articulation
articulation.p1: Staccato, accent, tenuto and marcato are a length and a weight. Staccato halves the note, accent adds weight, marcato does both, and tenuto is the full length the note already had.
articulation.p2: Shortening never moves anything. A staccato note releases early but still occupies its written length, so every following note stays where it was and the bar still adds up.

ornaments.heading: Ornaments
ornaments.p1: Trill, mordent, inverted mordent and turn are signs, not the notes they stand for. How an ornament is realised depends on period and taste, so the sign is stored and left readable.
ornaments.p2: Ornaments are notational here: they are drawn and they export, but playback does not realise them into notes.

grace.heading: Grace notes
grace.p1: A grace note hangs off the note it decorates rather than taking time from the bar, so it moves, copies and deletes with its principal and never makes a bar fail to add up.
grace.p2: They do sound. A grace note borrows from its principal rather than from the bar — capped at half its length — so every following note stays exactly where it was.

tuplets.heading: Tuplets
tuplets.p1: A triplet is not stored, it is recognised: three notes each two thirds of a plain value are a triplet, and are drawn as one. Change one of the three and the bracket simply stops being drawn, which is the truth rather than a stale mark.
tuplets.p2: Only whole threes group. A run of four is one triplet and a leftover, and rests count as members — a triplet with a rest in the middle is still a triplet.

beams.heading: Beams
beams.p1: Beaming is derived from the note values and the meter, so it follows the beat without being told. Only your disagreement is stored: break starts a new group at a note, and none takes a note out of beaming so it draws its flag.
beams.p2: Break is what vocal writing needs, where the beam follows the syllables rather than the beat. There is deliberately no join — beaming across a beat is the one change this cannot express.

lyrics.heading: Lyrics
lyrics.p1: Lyrics are typed through the line rather than one field at a time. Press L and type: space ends a word, a hyphen ends a syllable within one, Enter finishes, and Shift+space steps back over a typo.
lyrics.p2: Whether a syllable begins, continues or ends a word is worked out from those keystrokes rather than asked for. That is what draws the trailing hyphen and what fills the syllable type on export.
lyrics.p3: A syllable belongs to its note, so it moves, copies and deletes with the note it sits under.

chords.heading: Chord symbols
chords.p1: A chord symbol is stored exactly as you type it. C-7, Cmin7 and Cm7 are one chord written three ways, and none of them is rewritten or refused.
chords.p2: It prints above the stave — the opposite side from lyrics and dynamics, which is what keeps all three legible on a lead sheet. Only the root is parsed on export; the rest travels as the text you wrote.

spans.heading: Marks over several notes
spans.p1: A slur phrases a run of different pitches and joins nothing. Select two or more notes and press S. Fewer than two is refused — a phrase mark over one note means nothing.
spans.p2: A glissando slides between two notes; an octave bracket moves a passage up or down an octave on the page without changing what it sounds.
spans.p3: An octave bracket is a display lens, not a transposition. The score always stores sounding pitch, so 8va means these were written an octave lower to keep them on the stave.

playback.title: Playback
playback.summary: The transport, the piano keyboard, and how the view follows.

transport.heading: The transport
transport.p1: Space plays and pauses. The transport bar also carries stop, step by a bar either way, loop, a metronome, playback speed, tempo and the master volume.
transport.p2: The first press of play has a soundfont to fetch and hand to the synthesiser, which takes a few seconds. The transport does not claim to be playing until a note can actually sound, and shows the loading progress meanwhile.
transport.p3: The score cannot be edited while the transport is playing — except for mixing. Mute, solo, volume and pan stay live, because muting a part while listening to it is how an arrangement gets listened to.

keyboard.heading: The piano keyboard
keyboard.p1: Below the score is a full-width keyboard showing the active track's sounding notes as they play. Its range is the active track's instrument, not always all 88 keys, so it follows a track change and an instrument change alike.
keyboard.p2: It is an input device as well as a display. Pressing a key auditions it; releasing writes a note at the caret whose length is how long you held the key, snapped to a value the duration buttons could also have produced.
keyboard.p3: On a drum track every key is labelled with its drum, black keys included, because a drum map has no pattern to learn the way a keyboard does.

following.heading: Following the music
following.p1: The view follows playback without fighting your own scrolling. In page layout it keeps your offset into the system as the music wraps to the next one, so the track you are watching stays where you put it.
following.p2: In continuous layout it follows sideways instead, and clears the track gutter as it goes so the playing bar is never parked behind the track names.

settings.title: Settings
settings.summary: Appearance, how pitch is shown, and the developer options.

appearance.heading: Appearance
appearance.p1: Theme can follow your system or be pinned to light or dark, and the text size can be adjusted. Both apply across the whole app, including the score.
appearance.p2: The engraved score has its own colours for each role — a normal note, a selected one, one that was just generated, one that is sounding — and they follow the theme.

pitch.heading: Written or sounding pitch
pitch.p1: Transposing instruments can be shown either as they sound or as their player reads them. A B-flat trumpet part written at concert pitch looks a whole tone different from the part the player holds.
pitch.p2: This changes the display only. The score always stores sounding pitch, so switching the setting never edits a note.
pitch.p3: Note entry inverts the display before storing, so clicking a staff in written mode stores the pitch that will actually sound. Without that a part could look right and sound a whole tone out.

developer.heading: Developer mode
developer.p1: Developer mode adds diagnostics: performance measurements, a benchmark, and a diagnostics export useful when reporting a problem.
developer.p2: It changes nothing about the music. It is off by default and safe to leave on.

sharing.title: Snapshots and sharing
sharing.summary: Keeping versions, and publishing one for other people.

snapshots.heading: Snapshots
snapshots.p1: A snapshot is a copy of the score as it is now, kept under a name you choose. Your current work is saved first, so a snapshot always pins what you can actually see.
snapshots.p2: History is a tree rather than a list. Opening an older snapshot while a newer one exists does not destroy the newer one — it branches, and the next snapshot you take is a child of the one you opened.
snapshots.p3: Snapshots cannot be edited or deleted. That is enforced by there being no way to do it, rather than by a rule somebody has to remember.

publish.heading: Publishing
publish.p1: A snapshot can be published, which gives it a link anyone can open — no account needed. They get a reader that shows the score and plays it back, and nothing else.
publish.p2: Published work carries a name of its own, separate from the project name, and it is what appears on the Community page. You can change it later without touching the score.
publish.p3: Publishing asks you to confirm that the work is yours to share. Only what a published snapshot needs is ever sent — nothing about your account travels with it.

intro.heading: How they are arranged
intro.p1: Note entry keys deliberately take no modifier, so a shortcut belonging to your browser or your operating system can never be mistaken for a note. Bare letters write notes, digits choose note values.
intro.p2: That leaves Shift for the marks and Alt for the caret. The hairpin keys are the two nobody has to memorise, because Shift+< and Shift+> are the wedge symbols themselves.

structure.title: Bars and structure
structure.summary: Meter, key, barlines, repeats and the shape of the piece.

bars.heading: Bars
bars.p1: Click a bar number above a system to select that bar; shift-click another to select the span between them. That is how you aim Replace and regeneration, which both work on a range.
bars.p2: The bar grid is shared across tracks. A bar is the same bar on every stave, which is why anything that changes the grid applies to the whole score rather than one part.
bars.p3: Bar numbers skip a pickup, so the number the inspector shows, the number a player reads and the bar that go-to lands on are all the same number.

signatures.heading: Time and key
signatures.p1: Both are set per bar from the Bar tab, and both carry forward until something changes them. Setting a signature on bar 9 changes bar 9 onward, not the whole score.
signatures.p2: A key signature is stored as its position on the circle of fifths plus major or minor, but the inspector shows you the key name rather than the number.
signatures.p3: Changing the meter changes how long a bar is, so the notes already in it are refitted rather than silently overflowing.

pickup.heading: Pickup bars
pickup.p1: A pickup is a bar that is not counted. It is a flag on the first bar rather than a short bar mid-score, because a short bar in the middle of a piece is a deliberate irregular bar and keeps its number.
pickup.p2: It applies to every track, since a pickup on one stave only would be a score whose parts disagree about where bar 1 starts. It is offered on the first bar alone.

barlines.heading: Barlines
barlines.p1: A bar can carry a double or a final barline. Absent is the ordinary single line, which is almost every bar.
barlines.p2: Where a repeat and a double bar land on the same bar the repeat wins, in the drawing and in the export alike: a repeat is an instruction a player acts on, and drawing a double bar over it would silently remove it from the performance.

repeats.heading: Repeats and endings
repeats.p1: Repeat barlines are two independent marks rather than one span, because a closing repeat with no opening one repeats from the start of the piece — a real marking, not an error to prevent.
repeats.p2: Ending numbers are carried on every bar of a volta, and the bracket's ends are worked out from whether the neighbouring bar has the same numbers. Deleting a bar shortens the bracket instead of leaving one pointing at nothing.
repeats.p3: Repeats play. The score's own timing stays canonical and the transport works out the order the bars are actually performed in, so the caret, the scrubber and the bar readout never have to know repeats exist.

navigation.heading: D.C., D.S., Coda and Fine
navigation.p1: Segno, coda, To Coda and Fine are places a bar carries; the jump is the instruction, sitting on the bar at whose end it is obeyed. The six jumps are one choice rather than a direction plus a target, so only combinations a player actually meets can be written.
navigation.p2: The rule that is invisible in the notation: Fine and To Coda mean nothing on the way out. A player reads straight past both until a jump has sent them back.
navigation.p3: A jump is taken once — after obeying it the player reads through it — or the piece would never end. A broken marking still plays: a D.S. with no segno falls back to the start, as a reader would.

tempo.heading: Tempo
tempo.p1: The transport's tempo field always edits the tempo the piece starts at. The Bar tab's tempo sets a change at that bar, so a piece can slow down or shift at a rehearsal point.
tempo.p2: It shows the tempo in force, inherited from an earlier bar when this one sets none, so it is never blank and never lies. The starting tempo cannot be removed — a score with no tempo at all has no tempo.

clefs.heading: Clef changes
clefs.p1: A clef change is stored on the bar where it happens; absent means carry on with what is in force. A part that never changes clef stores nothing at all.
clefs.p2: It applies to one track, unlike repeats and barlines: a left hand crossing into treble says nothing about the right. Setting the clef already in force removes the marking rather than storing one that would print nothing.

tracks.title: Tracks and mixing
tracks.summary: Adding parts, choosing sounds, and balancing them.

adding.heading: Adding and removing
adding.p1: Add Track offers a blank track, a generated one, or one transcribed from an audio file. A new track gets the same bar grid as the score it joins.
adding.p2: A score always keeps at least one track, so the last one cannot be deleted. Deleting any other is a normal edit and undoes like one.

instrument.heading: Choosing a sound
instrument.p1: A track's sound is one of the 128 General MIDI programs, chosen from the Track tab. Changing it carries the existing notes into the new instrument's compass by whole octaves, so a bassline still reads as that bassline.
instrument.p2: If the part is wider than the new instrument can play, the change is refused with an explanation rather than half-applied.
instrument.p3: On a percussion track the same field chooses a drum kit instead. The two never agree: the number that means Brush as a kit means Violin as an instrument.

mixing.heading: Volume, pan, mute and solo
mixing.p1: Each track has a volume and a pan, and can be muted or soloed. These are the one kind of edit that stays available while the transport is playing, because muting a part while listening is how an arrangement gets listened to.
mixing.p2: Solo is exclusive: soloing a second track clears the first. You solo to hear one part, and a second solo would silently widen what you are hearing.
mixing.p3: Soloing also makes that track active, so every other track dims. Otherwise the silence has no face — you would hear one part with nothing on screen saying why.

visibility.heading: Hiding tracks
visibility.p1: A track can be hidden from the score without being deleted or muted. Hiding is about the page, not the sound.
visibility.p2: Exporting a score with hidden tracks asks whether to include them rather than quietly deciding.

active.heading: The active track
active.p1: One track is always the active one. It is the track notes are written to, the track the piano keyboard shows, and the one that stays at full strength while the others dim.
active.p2: Clicking anywhere on a track's staff makes it active. If the active track is deleted, the first track takes over rather than leaving nothing selected.

importAudio.description: Turns a recording into a project, split into parts — vocals, drums, bass, guitar, piano and the rest, each on its own track. It runs on the server and takes a few minutes, so the project appears straight away and fills itself in when it is done. Expect a sketch to edit, not a copy of the record. {{formats}}.

resources.title: Resources
resources.intro: Free music you can bring straight into {{appName}}, grouped by the importer each kind of file feeds. Download a file, then use Import on the projects page.

scores.title: Sheet music
scores.route: Import → MusicXML. Notes, rhythm, lyrics, dynamics and layout all survive the trip.

midi.title: MIDI files
midi.route: Import → MIDI. Notes and timing arrive; barlines and key are estimated, so the wizard lets you correct them.

modules.title: Tracker modules
modules.route: Import → Module. MOD, S3M, XM, IT and MPTM, chosen by what is inside the file rather than by its extension.

audio.title: Recordings to transcribe
audio.route: Import → Audio. One line at a time — transcription is monophonic, so pick a solo instrument or voice.

datasets.title: Bulk collections
datasets.route: Import → MIDI or MusicXML. Whole corpora rather than single pieces — download the archive, then open one file from it.

sound.title: Instruments and sound
sound.route: Not importable. These are the samples and SoundFonts behind playback, useful if you want to hear a score somewhere else.

reference.title: Formats and tools
reference.route: Reference, not files. What each format actually holds, and what else can open it.

link.musescore: Over a million community scores. The public-domain ones download as MusicXML.

link.imslp: The public-domain library of classical scores — 200,000 works, many with MusicXML beside the PDF.
link.cpdl: ChoralWiki: 40,000 choral and vocal scores, much of it with editable source files.
link.mutopia: Retypeset public-domain scores, with LilyPond source and MIDI alongside every entry.
link.musopenScores: Sheet music released with no copyright restrictions at all, beside Musopen's recordings.
link.openGoldberg: Bach's Goldberg Variations, score and performance both released for any use.
link.musicxmlDirectory: The format's own list of sites publishing MusicXML — where to look after this page.
link.bitmidi: A large searchable MIDI collection you can play in the browser before downloading.
link.vgmusic: Video game music sequenced by hand, sorted by console and by title.
link.kunstderfuge: The biggest classical MIDI archive on the web, thousands of files free to take.
link.midiworld: Classical, pop and game MIDI side by side, plus drum patterns.
link.mfiles: Well-sequenced MIDI of the classical pieces most people are looking for.
link.classicalArchives: A curated free set you may copy and use without asking permission.
link.theSession: Irish traditional tunes, every setting downloadable as MIDI.
link.hymnary: Hymn tunes and texts, most carrying MIDI of the full harmonisation.
link.midkar: Jazz, blues, ragtime and standards, sequenced over three decades.
link.modarchive: Tens of thousands of modules from the demoscene era onward, with a player built in.
link.modland: The deep archive: every tracker format, filed by composer, browsable as a drive.
link.amp: The Amiga scene's own catalogue, indexed by the people who wrote the music.
link.sceneOrg: The demoscene's file server. The music directory holds decades of party entries.
link.woolyss: A maintained index of where tracker music lives and what still plays it.
link.archiveTrackers: A curated multi-gigabyte set of MOD, XM, IT and S3M as a single download.
link.musopenAudio: Classical performances recorded and released into the public domain.
link.freeMusicArchive: Over 100,000 tracks under Creative Commons, filterable by licence.
link.freesound: Single notes, short phrases and field recordings, all openly licensed.
link.archiveAudio: Live concerts, 78rpm transfers and community uploads, free to download.
link.pdmx: A quarter of a million public-domain MusicXML scores, packaged as one dataset.
link.lakh: 176,000 MIDI files gathered for music research and free to download.
link.maestro: 200 hours of competition piano performances, MIDI aligned to the audio.
link.adlPiano: Piano MIDI filed by genre, sub-genre and artist.
link.museTrainer: A repository of public-domain piano MusicXML — clone it and open any file.
link.womenComposers: Scores by women composers, encoded and free to use.
link.freepats: Openly licensed instrument samples and patch sets.
link.polyphone: Free SoundFonts to download, and the editor to build your own.
link.generalUser: A General MIDI SoundFont tuned so all 128 programs sit together in one mix.
link.philharmonia: Every orchestral instrument, note by note, recorded by the orchestra itself.
link.musicXmlSpec: The MusicXML specification, element by element.
link.generalMidi: The 128-program sound set every track's instrument is chosen from.
link.standardMidiFile: What a .mid file actually contains, from the MIDI Association.
link.openMpt: The tracker to open a module in when you want its samples too.
link.verovio: Converts Humdrum-encoded scores to MusicXML in the browser.
